cards.front: What is cardiac output (Q), and how is it calculated using heart rate, stroke volume, and the Fick equation?
cards.back: Cardiac output (Q) is the volume of blood pumped by the heart per minute, calculated as Q = SV × HR. According to the Fick equation, oxygen uptake is expressed as VO2 = Q × a-vO2 difference.

cards.front: What physiological mechanism regulates the increase in stroke volume during acute aerobic exercise?
cards.back: The Frank-Starling mechanism regulates stroke volume: increased venous return expands end-diastolic volume (EDV), stretching myocardial fibers and increasing elastic recoil to pump a greater ejection fraction per beat.

cards.front: At what exercise intensity does stroke volume plateau, and what are normative peak values for untrained vs. trained individuals?
cards.back: Stroke volume plateaus at 40% to 50% of VO2max. Peak stroke volume averages 100 to 120 ml/beat in untrained men and 150 to 160 ml/beat in endurance-trained athletes (and is ∼25% lower in women).

cards.front: How does heart rate (HR) respond to increasing aerobic exercise intensity, and how is maximum heart rate (HRmax) estimated?
cards.back: Heart rate increases linearly with workload and oxygen consumption. Age-predicted HRmax is estimated as 220 - age (±10 to 12 bpm) or via the Tanaka formula: 208 - (0.7 × age).

cards.front: How do systolic and diastolic blood pressure respond during acute aerobic exercise, and what is the Rate-Pressure Product (RPP)?
cards.back:
• Systolic BP: Increases linearly from resting (110–139 mmHg) up to 220–260 mmHg at maximal exertion.
  • Diastolic BP: Remains stable or slightly decreases (60–89 mmHg).
  • Rate-Pressure Product (RPP): Calculated as HR × SBP to estimate myocardial workload.

cards.front: How is blood flow redistributed throughout the body from rest to maximal aerobic exercise?
cards.back: At rest, active skeletal muscle receives 15% to 20% of total cardiac output. During maximal exercise, selective vasoconstriction of visceral organs and vasodilation of muscle vascular beds redistributes up to 90% of cardiac output to working muscles.

cards.front: What components define minute ventilation (VE), and how does it adjust during acute aerobic exertion?
cards.back: Minute ventilation is calculated as VE = Tidal Volume (TV) × Breathing Frequency (fb). Resting VE (10–15 L/min) surges 15- to 25-fold up to 90 to 150 L/min during maximal exercise.

cards.front: What is the ventilatory equivalent for oxygen (VE / VO2), and why does it increase sharply at higher exercise intensities?
cards.back: VE / VO2 is the ratio of air ventilated to oxygen consumed (normally 20–25 L air / L O2). At high intensities (>45%–65% VO2max untrained, 70%–90% trained), it rises to 35–40 L air / L O2 to exhale excess CO2 produced from buffering metabolic lactic acid.

cards.front: How do partial pressures of O2 and CO2 in active muscle tissue change from rest to maximal exercise to drive diffusion?
cards.back:
Driven by pressure gradients:
  • PO2: Drops from 40 mmHg at rest down to 3 mmHg during maximal exercise in working muscle cells.
  • PCO2: Rises from 46 mmHg at rest up to 90 mmHg during maximal exercise.

cards.front: How is oxygen transported in the bloodstream during acute aerobic exercise?
cards.back: A small fraction (3 ml O2/L) is dissolved in plasma (establishing PO2), while the vast majority is bound to hemoglobin (1.34 ml O2 per gram of Hb), yielding ∼20 ml O2 per 100 ml of arterial blood in men.

cards.front: What is the primary mechanism for carbon dioxide (CO2) transport in arterial blood?
cards.back: Approximately 70% of CO2 is transported as bicarbonate (HCO3-) via the carbonic anhydrase reaction: CO2 + H2O ↔ H2CO3 ↔ H+ + HCO3-, accompanied by a chloride shift into red blood cells.
